items.title: What an audit report is actually for
items.summary: A fund that collects thousands of crores and spends lakhs is not a scandal by arithmetic alone. It is a question about intent.

body.text: The number is not the story

Every few months a figure surfaces that looks damning on its own: money in, very little money out. The gap gets a headline, the headline gets a hashtag, and the argument ends there. But a balance is not a verdict. Funds are allowed to hold money. Endowments are supposed to. The question an audit exists to answer is narrower and harder: was the money held for a stated purpose, and does the holding match that purpose?

Read the audit for three things. First, the mandate — what the fund said it would do with the money when it asked for it. Second, the disbursement schedule, which tells you whether slow spending was planned or simply happened. Third, the auditor's own language: statutory auditors are careful people, and a qualified opinion is a much louder signal than a large unspent balance.
Why this matters beyond one fund

Public money attracts two failures at once — the failure to spend it well, and the failure to scrutinise it well. A press cycle that treats every unspent rupee as theft trains readers to ignore the cases that are theft. Precision is not pedantry here. It is the only thing that makes the accusation mean anything when it is finally warranted.
